name: Ladder Mate
summary: The ladder mate uses two rooks working in alternation, one sealing off a rank while the other checks, marching the enemy king to the edge for checkmate.
intro: The ladder mate, also known as the lawnmower mate or staircase mate, is the classic method of checkmating a lone king with two rooks. The rooks take turns: one holds an entire rank, forming a wall the king cannot cross, while the other delivers check on the adjacent rank, forcing the king back one row. Repeating this rhythm walks the king to the edge of the board, where the final check leaves it no escape. It is one of the first mates every beginner learns, and unlike a queen-and-rook mate, the two rooks do the whole job by themselves.
boardCaption: The starting position: White rooks on a1 and b2 against the lone Black king on g7, ready to climb rank by rank with 1.Ra7+ and mate on the eighth rank.

sections.heading: How the Ladder Works
paragraphs: The mechanism is a simple division of labor. One rook parks itself on a rank and controls every square along it, walling the king off from that row entirely. The second rook then checks on the very next rank. The king cannot step back through the wall and cannot stay in check, so it must retreat one row toward the edge of the board. Nothing else is required: no king support, no other pieces.

Then the rooks swap roles. The rook that just checked becomes the new wall, holding its rank, while the other rook advances to check on the next one. Rung by rung, like feet climbing a ladder, the rooks alternate between controlling and checking, and the king is herded steadily backward. The pattern earns its nicknames: the ladder for the alternating rungs, the lawnmower for the way the rooks sweep across the board row by row.

sections.heading: Driving the King to the Edge
paragraphs: In the diagram, White has rooks on a1 and b2 against the Black king on g7. White begins with 1.Ra7+, the a1-rook swinging up to a7 to check along the seventh rank. The king cannot step down or sideways into the checking rook's rank; its only path leads upward, so it retreats with 1...Kg8, landing on the eighth rank at the edge of the board.

Now comes the finish: 2.Rb8#. The b2-rook climbs to b8 and checks along the eighth rank. The a7-rook still seals the seventh, so the king cannot come back down, and both rooks sit far away on the a- and b-files, well out of the king's reach. With no square to run to and no rook to capture, the Black king is checkmated on the edge it was driven to.

sections.heading: Keep the Rooks Safe
paragraphs: The one thing that can go wrong with the ladder is letting the enemy king get close enough to attack a rook. The cure is built into the technique: keep both rooks on files far from the king. In our example they operate from the a- and b-files while the king lives over on the g-file, so it can never touch them. Distance is the rooks' armor; their long reach means they control ranks just as well from far away.

If the king does march toward your rooks, do not panic and do not give up the wall. Simply swing the threatened rook to the far side of the board, all the way across its rank, where it keeps controlling exactly the same row from a safe distance. The ladder then resumes as if nothing happened. This little sidestep is the only finesse the pattern requires, which is why the two-rook mate is among the first techniques every player masters.

keyIdeas: Two rooks alternate roles: one walls off a rank while the other checks on the next, pushing the king back one row at a time.
The king is driven rank by rank to the edge of the board, where the final check is mate.
In the example, 1.Ra7+ forces 1...Kg8, and 2.Rb8# mates along the eighth rank while the a7-rook seals the seventh.
Keep both rooks on files far from the enemy king so it can never attack them.
If the king approaches a rook, swing that rook to the far side of the board and continue the ladder.
Also called the lawnmower or staircase mate, it needs no help from the king or any other piece.
